question: What term describes tissue damage caused by a lack of adequate blood supply?

options.A: Ischemia
options.B: Embolism
options.C: Edema
options.D: Hyperemia

explanation: Ischemia is the medical term for inadequate blood flow to a tissue or organ, depriving it of needed oxygen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h8)

question: When is the right time to start transmission-based precautions for a patient?

options.A: At the first sign of symptoms or upon suspicion of infection
options.B: After public health officers visit the ward
options.C: When the patient requests a private hospital room
options.D: Only after laboratory confirmation is fully finalized

explanation: Spot on! Waiting for lab results takes time, and germs don't wait. As soon as you suspect an infection, start precautions right away to keep everyone safe.

question: Most primary brain tumors start growing from which type of supportive cells in the nervous system?

options.A: Neurons
options.B: Glial cells
options.C: Bone cells
options.D: Blood vessels

explanation: Spot on! While neurons get all the fame for sending nerve signals, most primary brain tumors actually arise from glial cells—the supportive glue and caretaker cells of the brain.

question: Why do patients with long-standing chronic pancreatitis eventually develop diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Dietary restrictions force the body to rely entirely on stored body fat.
options.B: Scar tissue gradually destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.
options.C: The liver stops responding to insulin because it is overworked by fat digestion.
options.D: Chronic vomiting causes a permanent chemical imbalance in blood sugar.

explanation: You're doing great! As chronic inflammation forms scar tissue over time, it slowly wipes out the insulin-making cells in the islets of Langerhans, leading to diabetes.

question: What is the primary reason nursing pharmacology education became much more rigorous over the past century?

options.A: Patients no longer wanted to take natural remedies.
options.B: Modern medications became significantly more potent and complex, increasing risks.
options.C: Physicians stopped prescribing medications altogether.
options.D: Nurses took over the responsibility of manufacturing hospital drugs.

explanation: As drugs became more powerful, the potential for dangerous side effects and interactions grew, requiring nurses to possess advanced pharmacological knowledge to protect patients. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T1#GNS125_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of these is a clear example of a psychosocial hazard at work?

options.A: Bullying and harassment from a supervisor
options.B: A cut from an unsterilized scalpel
options.C: Lifting a heavy patient without help
options.D: Breathing in toxic welding fumes

explanation: Psychosocial hazards deal with workplace relationships, job pressure, and emotional stresses like bullying or heavy emotional demands.

question: Why is it so important to report a disease outbreak quickly in your community?

options.A: It guarantees free medical treatment for all citizens
options.B: It stops patients from visiting traditional healers
options.C: It helps health agencies spot unusual disease patterns early
options.D: It reduces the cost of prescription drugs in pharmacies

explanation: Spotting cases early gives health teams the heads-up they need to track trends and stop epidemics in their tracks. You're building solid public health sense!

question: Which of these is NOT a common complication of unmanaged maternal distress?

options.A: Increased need for emergency Caesarean birth
options.B: Postpartum psychological trauma
options.C: Dysfunctional or prolonged labour
options.D: Permanent loss of maternal vision

explanation: Vision loss doesn't happen just from stress during labour. The other options are very real risks when distress isn't managed!

question: Where does home health care primarily take place?

options.A: Inside the patient's place of residence
options.B: At a regional diagnostic laboratory
options.C: Inside a specialized surgical ward
options.D: At a primary health care clinic

explanation: You've got this! Home health care simply means bringing nursing and medical care right to where the patient lives. Easy peasy!

question: Which principle ensures that health services are affordable and located where young people can easily reach them?

options.A: Appropriateness
options.B: Accessibility
options.C: Acceptability
options.D: Equity

explanation: Spot on! Accessibility is all about removing financial, physical, and time barriers so young people can actually get to the clinic.

question: How is endocrine signaling different from nervous system signaling?

options.A: Nervous signaling produces much slower, permanent bodily changes
options.B: Nervous signaling relies entirely on circulating blood vessels
options.C: Endocrine signaling uses direct physical contact with cells
options.D: Endocrine signaling is slower and has longer-lasting effects

explanation: Nerve impulses are like a quick flash of lightning, while hormones are like a slow, steady wave whose effects linger much longer.

question: During a pelvic exam, what physical sign would you expect in a patient with Type II FGM?

options.A: A completely sealed vaginal opening with a tiny pinhole
options.B: An intact hymen with no external scars
options.C: Extensive scar tissue and absence of the labia minora
options.D: Enlarged, hypertrophied Bartholin glands

explanation: Well done! The removal of both the clitoris and labia minora leaves clear signs of scar tissue and missing external structures.

question: Why does the blood-brain barrier present a major hurdle when treating certain brain infections?

options.A: It actively destroys all types of antibiotics in the blood
options.B: It prevents many helpful medicines from entering brain tissue
options.C: It increases the pressure of cerebrospinal fluid dangerously
options.D: It allows bacteria to hide safely inside the ventricles

explanation: The same tight barriers that keep harmful toxins out also block many beneficial pharmaceutical drugs from reaching infections inside the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h7)

question: Why must a nurse know the difference between traditional scarification and self-harm scars?

options.A: To ensure the client is charged the correct hospital fees
options.B: To report the family to the local village chief
options.C: To guide appropriate medical treatment and mental health support
options.D: To decide which type of antibiotic ointment to sell

explanation: Exactly! Understanding where scars come from helps you provide the right physical care and emotional support tailored to your patient.

question: If a patient mentions they first visited a traditional or spiritual healer before coming to the hospital, how should a nurse respond?

options.A: Scold the patient and family for engaging in unscientific practices
options.B: Refuse to treat the patient until they sign a formal apology letter
options.C: Acknowledge the patient's choices respectfully while offering safe, evidence-based medical care
options.D: Pretend that traditional healing practices do not exist in the community

explanation: Respecting a patient's background builds great trust. We don't judge their journey; instead, we warmly offer safe, professional medical care from that point on.

question: Why are shellfish like shrimp and crabs not allowed in a traditional kosher diet?

options.A: They are classified as land animals
options.B: They are harvested during forbidden months
options.C: They consume blood from other marine life
options.D: They lack fins and scales

explanation: According to kosher rules, acceptable seafood must have both fins and scales, which rules out bottom-feeding shellfish like crabs and shrimp.

question: A newborn is diagnosed with anencephaly. Which part of the embryo's neural tube failed to close?

options.A: Caudal spinal cord
options.B: Neural crest cells
options.C: Anterior neuropore
options.D: Posterior neuropore

explanation: You got it! Anencephaly happens when the top end (anterior neuropore) of the neural tube doesn't close properly, affecting brain development.

question: What is a key responsibility of nurses in preventing the continuation of breast ironing?

options.A: Educating communities and advocating against harmful traditions
options.B: Imposing heavy financial fines on families who practice it
options.C: Passing strict national laws in parliamentary meetings
options.D: Managing hospital budgets for surgical equipment

explanation: Nurses play a major role in teaching communities about the dangers of the practice and promoting safe parenting. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T17#GNS312_U1_T17_h8)

question: Why does the mother's blood system change so much early in pregnancy?

options.A: To support the growing fetus and uteroplacental blood flow
options.B: To compensate for a sudden loss of red blood cells
options.C: To lower body temperature during the first trimester
options.D: To prepare the mother for heavy physical exercise

explanation: Great job! These adaptations ensure the developing baby and placenta get enough oxygen and nutrients.

question: How does a new mother's body mainly get rid of extra pregnancy fluids right after birth?

options.A: Through increased production of bile acids
options.B: Through reabsorption into the bone marrow
options.C: Through heavy urination and sweating
options.D: Through rapid shedding of stomach lining

explanation: Peeing and sweating a lot in the first few days postpartum is totally normal—it's just the body's way of flushing out the extra pregnancy fluids!

question: In which layer of the uterus do fibroids usually start growing?

options.A: Myometrium
options.B: Endometrium
options.C: Perimetrium
options.D: Cervix

explanation: The myometrium is the thick muscular middle layer of the uterus, which makes it the perfect home for fibroids to develop.

question: Why should a nurse carefully monitor weight and calorie intake for a patient on a strict low-fat diet?

options.A: Weight tracking is the only reliable way to measure liver enzyme levels
options.B: Monitoring calories prevents the sudden development of high blood pressure
options.C: Patients on fat-free diets almost always develop rapid fluid retention and edema
options.D: Strict fat limits can easily lead to unintentional weight loss and inadequate calorie intake

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Removing fat drops food energy fast, putting patients at risk of unintended weight loss.

question: How do vitamins and minerals often help enzymes do their work?

options.A: They turn into glucose to provide extra energy for the brain.
options.B: They act as coenzymes and cofactors to help enzymes function.
options.C: They slow down metabolism to prevent the body from overheating.
options.D: They replace enzymes when the body runs out of protein.

explanation: Many vitamins and minerals team up with enzymes as coenzymes or cofactors, acting like a key that unlocks the enzyme's full working potential!

question: You notice a patient has dry, brittle hair, pale skin, and spoon-shaped nails. What part of the nutritional assessment is this?

options.A: Dietary history recall
options.B: Clinical observations
options.C: Biochemical tests
options.D: Anthropometric tracking

explanation: When you look directly at the patient's body for physical signs of nutrition issues, you are doing a clinical observation!

question: Why do women often lose bone density after reaching menopause?

options.A: High FSH destroys the bone marrow
options.B: Lower estrogen levels remove the protective effect on bones
options.C: The uterus stops making calcium
options.D: Lack of progesterone stops water absorption

explanation: Correct! Estrogen helps keep bones strong, so when it drops after menopause, the risk of weak bones (osteoporosis) goes up.

question: A patient has an injury affecting the clear gel that fills the main cavity behind the lens. What is this gel called?

options.A: The vitreous humor
options.B: The corneal stroma
options.C: The pupillary fluid
options.D: The aqueous humor

explanation: The vitreous humor is the jelly-like substance that gives the eyeball its stable shape behind the lens. Keep up the good work!

question: A pregnant patient with gestational diabetes maintains a fasting blood glucose of 6.1 mmol/L despite following her diet and exercise plan for two weeks. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Advise the patient to eliminate all carbohydrates
options.B: Continue diet and exercise for another trimester
options.C: Stop all monitoring to reduce patient anxiety
options.D: Initiate pharmacotherapy such as insulin

explanation: When lifestyle changes fail to reach target blood glucose levels within a short timeframe, medication must be started to protect the baby from high sugar. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h5)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with recurring kidney stones and severe flank pain. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to visualize the exact location of the stones in the ureters?

options.A: Intravenous pyelogram
options.B: Electrocardiogram
options.C: Pulmonary function test
options.D: Echocardiogram

explanation: An IVP uses contrast dye to highlight the urinary tract, making it very effective for spotting kidney stones causing flank pain. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: How much water should a nurse use to flush a gastrostomy tube between different medications?

options.A: 15 to 30 mL of warm water
options.B: 100 to 200 mL of ice water
options.C: 1 to 2 mL of sterile saline
options.D: No water should ever be used

explanation: Flushing with warm water between each medication clears residual drug from the tube and prevents dangerous chemical reactions or clogs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h6)

question: How do lab staff figure out if an antibiotic can kill a specific bacterium on a test plate?

options.A: By counting how many days the culture plate sat inside the incubator
options.B: By observing if the entire agar plate changes to a bright red color
options.C: By checking the expiration date printed on the exterior box of disks
options.D: By measuring the clear ring of no growth around the antibiotic disk

explanation: That clear halo around the antibiotic disk is called the zone of inhibition. The bigger the ring, the better the drug works!

question: A patient insists on receiving an injection for a mild headache instead of taking paracetamol tablets. What drives this demand?

options.A: A diagnosed severe allergy to all oral analgesic medications
options.B: Cultural perception that needles equal superior medical treatment
options.C: Hospital protocol requiring injections for all reported pain
options.D: Immediate renal failure requiring rapid parenteral hydration

explanation: Patients often associate the physical action of an injection with high-value care, leading to unnecessary demands. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is the main chemical messenger released by postganglionic sympathetic fibers onto target organs?

options.A: Serotonin
options.B: Dopamine
options.C: Norepinephrine
options.D: Acetylcholine

explanation: Norepinephrine is the classic helper that sympathetic neurons use to talk to your heart, blood vessels, and other target organs during stress.

question: Why isn't just treating sick patients enough to stop a waterborne disease outbreak?

options.A: The environmental reservoir remains contaminated and causes reinfection
options.B: Waterborne pathogens cannot be killed by boiling
options.C: Antibiotics do not work against bacteria found in water
options.D: Patients always become asymptomatic carriers after recovery

explanation: If you don't fix the dirty water supply, people will keep drinking it and falling right back sick. You've got to fix the source!

question: Which viral enzyme helps convert HIV's single-stranded RNA into double-stranded DNA?

options.A: Integrase
options.B: Amylase
options.C: Reverse transcriptase
options.D: Protease

explanation: Reverse transcriptase is the clever enzyme HIV uses to turn its RNA into DNA inside the host cell.

question: What is the main reason a nurse performs an eye irrigation?

options.A: To flush out chemicals or foreign bodies from the eye
options.B: To deliver antibiotic eye drops for a bacterial infection
options.C: To permanently dilate the pupil for a detailed eye exam
options.D: To measure the exact intraocular pressure of the globe

explanation: Great job thinking practically! Irrigation uses a steady stream of fluid to wash away dangerous substances or particles before they hurt the eye tissues. You've got this!

question: How do farmers' markets help build trust between buyers and their food?

options.A: By ensuring that all food items are processed in distant factories
options.B: By hiding the origin of the produce to protect trade secrets
options.C: By shipping all unsold food to foreign countries
options.D: By allowing buyers to ask growers directly about farming methods

explanation: Correct! Chatting face-to-face with the person who grew your food creates amazing transparency and peace of mind.

question: Why might doctors order a thyroid test for a patient with severe hyperemesis?

options.A: It helps check the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.B: Thyroid failure is the primary cause of all pregnancy vomiting
options.C: High levels of hCG can temporarily stimulate the thyroid gland
options.D: Thyroid medication is always used to cure morning sickness

explanation: Because hCG hormone looks a bit like thyroid-stimulating hormone, sky-high pregnancy hormones can trick the thyroid into working overtime. Brilliant clinical insight!
